title: Prehistoric Caucasus
subtitle: 1,850,000–3,500 BC · Dmanisi, the Caucasus Hunter-Gatherers and the First Winemakers

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: No rulers, only horizons — the first hominins at Dmanisi, cave hunters, the Kura-valley farming villages and the Chalcolithic communities

entries.label: Azokh and Azykh — a cave with a mandible
entries.hint: The cave, called Azokh by Armenians and Azykh by Azerbaijanis, has produced Acheulean hand-axes, the bones of cave bears and other animals, and a human lower jaw found in 1968 that has been assigned to Homo heidelbergensis or an early Neanderthal. Several dating studies disagree, and the Lower Palaeolithic sequence is placed anywhere between about 700,000 and 200,000 years ago; the jaw is usually put toward the later end. An international team has worked there since 2002.
entries.note: M. Huseynov (1968 mandible find); Y. Fernández-Jalvo et al. (eds), Azokh Cave and the Transcaucasian Corridor (2016).

entries.label: Dmanisi — the earliest humans outside Africa
entries.hint: At the foot of a medieval fortress in southern Georgia, excavators from 1983 on have uncovered the remains of several early Homo individuals, five well-preserved skulls among them, together with stone tools and the bones of the animals they butchered. Dated to some 1.8 million years ago, they are the oldest well-dated hominins found outside Africa. Their small brains, around 550–780 cubic centimetres, and their mixture of primitive and modern traits make them a key case for the early dispersal of humans.
entries.note: D. Lordkipanidze et al., 'A complete skull from Dmanisi, Georgia, and the evolutionary biology of early Homo', Science 342 (2013); Gabunia and Vekua, Nature 373 (1995); Garcia et al., Quaternary Geochronology (2010).

entries.label: Nor Geghi 1 — early Levallois technology
entries.hint: In the Hrazdan gorge north of Yerevan, stratified tools lying between volcanic layers dated by argon methods show a shift in the middle of the Middle Pleistocene from large bifacial hand-axes to flakes struck from prepared cores. The site is one of the earliest places where the Levallois technique and the Acheulean are found together, and it was reported in 2014 to push the Lower-to-Middle Palaeolithic change in the region back well before 200,000 years ago.
entries.note: D. S. Adler et al., 'Early Levallois technology and the Lower to Middle Paleolithic transition in the Southern Caucasus', Science 345 (2014).

entries.label: Dzudzuana Cave — the cave hunters of the Upper Palaeolithic
entries.hint: In the foothills of Imereti, modern human hunters left layers of stone blades and bone points, the remains of ibex and aurochs, and in the cave's lowest levels, fibres of wild flax which had been spun and dyed in several colours, among the oldest such textile traces in the world. A genome from the cave's later layers, of about 26,000 years ago, belongs to a population ancestral to many in West Asia.
entries.note: E. Kvavadze et al., '30,000-year-old wild flax fibers', Science 325 (2009); I. Lazaridis et al., 'Genomic insights into the origin of farming in the ancient Near East', Nature 536 (2016); I. Lazaridis et al., bioRxiv (2018) and Science 377 (2022).

entries.label: The Mousterian caves of Imereti and Armenia
entries.hint: In the limestone caves of Imereti and the Armenian highlands, among them Ortvale Klde, Djruchula, Kudaro and Hovk-1, Middle Palaeolithic hunters left Mousterian tools and the bones of ibex, bison and deer, killed and butchered at the cave mouths. Neanderthal remains have been identified in the South Caucasus in only a few caves.
entries.note: V. Liubin and A. Cherniakhovsky, Kudaro excavation reports; Pinhasi et al., 'Revised age of late Neanderthal occupation' PNAS (2011), for the neighbouring northern Caucasus; Hovk-1 excavation reports.

entries.label: The Caucasus hunter-gatherers at Satsurblia and Kotias Klde
entries.hint: Genomes from two individuals, one of about 13,300 years ago from Satsurblia Cave and one of about 9,700 years ago from Kotias Klde, define a genetic population of 'Caucasus hunter-gatherers' which had been isolated in the region during the Last Glacial Maximum. The ancestry is also found in the later peoples of the steppe and of Iran and Anatolia.
entries.note: C. Jones et al., 'Upper Palaeolithic genomes reveal deep roots of modern Eurasians', Nature Communications 6 (2015).

entries.group: Neolithic Villages of the Kura and Araxes
entries.label: The Shulaveri-Shomu culture
entries.loc: Shulaveris Gora and Aruchlo, Kvemo Kartli
entries.hint: The earliest farming villages of the middle Kura valley, Shulaveris Gora, Aruchlo, Imiris Gora and Gadachrili Gora in Georgia and Göytepe and Hacı Elamxanlı Tepe in Azerbaijan, were built of round mudbrick houses with domed roofs, with crops of wheat, barley and grapes and herds of cattle, sheep and goats, and with tools of obsidian from the nearby volcanic sources. The culture is now dated from the early sixth millennium BC.
entries.note: C. Chataigner et al., 'The Neolithic of the Caucasus', Oxford Handbooks Online (2014); S. Hansen et al., Aruchlo excavation reports (Deutsches Archäologisches Institut, 2007–).

entries.group: Neolithic Villages of the Kura and Araxes
entries.label: Aratashen and Aknashen — the villages of the Ararat plain
entries.hint: At Aratashen and the neighbouring Aknashen, on the Araxes plain below Mount Ararat, early farmers built round houses of mudbrick and reed, grew emmer wheat and barley, kept cattle, sheep and goats, and worked flaked obsidian from the Gegham and Aragats volcanoes. Their culture is closely related to that of the Kura sites of the Shulaveri-Shomu type.
entries.note: R. Badalyan, C. Chataigner et al., Aratashen reports (2004–); Arimura et al., Aknashen reports (2010).

entries.label: The Sioni culture and the Chalcolithic of Kartli
entries.hint: In the fifth and fourth millennia the villages of eastern Georgia, among them Sioni itself, kept their houses of mudbrick but used copper and stone in increasing amounts, with burnished pottery and herds of cattle and sheep. The Sioni phase marks the Chalcolithic of the Kura basin and the ground out of which the Kura-Araxes culture grew.
entries.note: G. Palumbi, The Red and the Black (2008); Georgian National Museum, Sioni culture studies.

entries.label: Leyla Tepe — a Karabakh settlement in contact with Mesopotamia
entries.hint: The settlement of Leyla Tepe, on the Karabakh steppe, has houses of mudbrick and walls with plastered floors, painted pottery influenced by the Mesopotamian Ubaid style, and early copper objects. Its excavators saw it as a link between the Mesopotamian world and the Kura-Araxes culture which followed; others point out that the dating and the Ubaid link remain uncertain.
entries.note: I. Narimanov, Kultura drevneishego zemledelcheskogo i skotovodcheskogo naseleniia Azerbaidzhana (1987); T. Akhundov on Leyla Tepe.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The Neanderthal horizon and a long evidentiary gap on violence

entries.label: The last Neanderthals and the first modern humans
entries.hint: Neanderthals, who had lived in the Caucasus caves for over a hundred thousand years, are found there until about 40,000 years ago, and anatomically modern humans with Upper Palaeolithic blade tools appear within a few thousand years in sites such as Ortvale Klde. The nature of the meeting, whether replacement, mixing or both, is not known from the Caucasus data and is a subject of debate.
entries.note: Pinhasi et al., 'Revised age of late Neanderthal occupation' PNAS (2011); Bar-Yosef and Belfer-Cohen on the Caucasus Upper Palaeolithic.

entries.label: Violence in the archaeological record
entries.hint: The Neolithic and Chalcolithic villages show no walls, weapon caches or mass graves, and few skeletal injuries have been published; the first fortified settlements and weapon-rich burials belong to the Kura-Araxes and later periods. The record is thin, however, and the absence of evidence should not be taken as peace.
entries.note: Review in Chataigner et al. 2014; Palumbi 2008.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Round-house villages without palaces, and the evidence for who stored what

entries.label: The round-house villages
entries.hint: The villages of the Kura valley were compact settlements of 20 or 30 round mudbrick houses of similar size, with courtyards and storage pits, and no palace or temple distinguishes any one household. The layout suggests small kin-based communities, with food shared and stored by households, though conclusions are drawn from few excavated sites.
entries.note: S. Hansen, Aruchlo excavation reports; Chataigner et al. 2014.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Rock carvings at Gobustan and Ughtasar, burial under houses and the ritual cave at Areni

entries.label: Gobustan
entries.hint: On a rocky plateau by the Caspian south of Baku, some 6,000 petroglyphs, caves and rock shelters record human use from at least the Mesolithic to the Middle Ages: figures of hunters and dancers, bulls, deer and reed boats, and later symbols and inscriptions. UNESCO listed the site in 2007. The dating of the oldest carvings is uncertain, and some claims of tens of thousands of years are not generally accepted.
entries.note: UNESCO World Heritage List no. 1076 (2007); Jafarzadeh, Gobustan rock art (1973, 1999).

entries.label: The dead beneath the floors
entries.hint: In the Neolithic villages of both the Kura and Araxes plains the dead, often infants and children, were buried in pits under or beside the house floors, in a flexed position and sometimes with ochre, beads or a pot. The practice binds the house with the family and its ancestors.
entries.note: Badalyan et al. on Aratashen and Aknashen; Hansen on Aruchlo.

entries.label: Areni-1 — a ritual cave
entries.hint: The cave Areni-1, on the Arpa river, was used by the late Chalcolithic community both as a ritual place and for burials, in which the dead, among them children, were placed in large clay jars or shallow pits, sometimes with a skull set in a bowl. The cave's dry and cool conditions preserved leather, cloth, wood and plant remains of extraordinary rarity.
entries.note: B. Gasparyan et al., Areni-1 excavation reports (2008–); K. Wilkinson et al., Journal of Field Archaeology 37 (2012).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Boats and figures cut into stone, painted and burnished pottery

entries.label: Ughtasar
entries.hint: On the high volcanic plateau of Ughtasar in the Syunik mountains, at about 3,300 metres, thousands of carved figures cover basalt boulders around a seasonal lake: goats, deer, hunters, wheeled vehicles, dancers and symbols. They were probably made by herders in summer camp, over a long period from the Mesolithic or Neolithic to the Bronze Age; none can be dated closely.
entries.note: Armenian Academy of Sciences, Institute of Archaeology and Ethnography, Ughtasar surveys; Armenian rock-art studies.

entries.label: The pottery of the Kura villages
entries.hint: The Shulaveri-Shomu villages made pottery by hand from clay tempered with chaff, in simple forms such as bowls and jars, with some burnished and some bearing incised or plastic decoration. A fine, painted ware appears in the following Chalcolithic at Leyla Tepe, in a style comparable with the Ubaid ware of the south.
entries.note: Chataigner et al. 2014; Narimanov 1987.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: A skull that reopened the human family tree, and a stone circle read as a sky record

entries.label: Dmanisi and the single-species hypothesis
entries.hint: The fifth Dmanisi skull, published in 2013, is large-jawed and small-brained, whereas other skulls from the site differ greatly in their size and form. The excavators argued that the variation was within the range of one population, and that the fossils currently named as several early Homo species could instead be variants of one lineage. The claim is debated among palaeoanthropologists.
entries.note: Lordkipanidze et al., Science 342 (2013), with the discussion that followed in the palaeoanthropological literature.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Cattle, sheep and wheat in the Kura valley, the earliest winemaking, and obsidian and copper

entries.label: Wheat, barley and the first herds
entries.hint: The first farmers of the South Caucasus grew emmer, bread wheat and barley, and kept cattle, sheep and goats, with pigs and fewer wild animals; storage pits and clay bins show the harvest was kept for the year. Plant and animal domesticates reached the region from Mesopotamia and the Zagros and Anatolia by the early sixth millennium.
entries.note: Chataigner et al. 2014; Lyonnet et al. on Hacı Elamxanlı Tepe.

entries.label: The earliest winemaking
entries.hint: Grape pips and chemical residues in clay jars of Gadachrili Gora and Khramis Didi Gora in Georgia, from about 6000 BC, have been read as evidence of wine made in the Neolithic, the oldest known; at Areni-1 in Armenia, around 4100 BC, a pressing platform, fermentation vats and storage jars make up a full wine-making installation. The Caucasus is accordingly claimed as an early centre of viticulture.
entries.note: P. McGovern et al., PNAS 114 (2017); Barnard et al., 'Chemical evidence for wine production around 4000 BCE in the Late Chalcolithic Near Eastern highlands', Journal of Archaeological Science (2011).

entries.label: The obsidian trade
entries.hint: Obsidian from the volcanic sources of the Gegham and Aragats mountains in Armenia and from Chikiani in Georgia was made into blades and arrowheads for the farming villages, and chemical analysis finds it hundreds of kilometres away along the Kura and Araxes. Obsidian was the one material of the region traded in bulk.
entries.note: Badalyan, Chataigner et al., obsidian sourcing studies; Blackman et al. on Caucasus obsidian.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Pebble tools, Levallois flakes, mudbrick, the wine press and the oldest known leather shoe

entries.label: The Oldowan tools of Dmanisi
entries.hint: Thousands of choppers, cores and flakes of local basalt and andesite, struck from river cobbles, lie in the Dmanisi deposits with butchered animal bones. They are an Oldowan type of tool, as in East Africa, and show that the first people outside Africa had not yet the bifacial hand-axe.
entries.note: Gabunia, Vekua et al., Science 288 (2000); Mgeladze et al., on Dmanisi lithics.

entries.label: The mine at Sakdrisi
entries.hint: Georgian and German archaeologists found at Sakdrisi, in the hills of Kvemo Kartli, a hillside mine of stone-hammered galleries and the stone hammers used to break out gold-bearing quartz, which they argued dated to the fourth millennium BC, and possibly to the middle of the fifth. The dating is disputed, and the hill was damaged by modern gold mining in 2013–2014.
entries.note: T. Stöllner et al., Sakdrisi excavations (2005–); I. Gambashidze et al. (eds), Georgien: Schätze aus dem Land des Goldenen Vlies (2001).

entries.label: The winepress and vats of Areni-1
entries.hint: In the cave's chalcolithic level excavators found a shallow clay-lined basin used as a press, with a drain into a buried vat, a fermentation vessel and storage jars, along with dried grape skins, pressed grape remains and vine twigs. The installation seems to have been made for processing wine, and perhaps for ritual use as well.
entries.note: Barnard et al. 2011; Gasparyan et al. 2014.

entries.label: The Areni shoe
entries.hint: A single shoe of cow hide, sewn up the heel and laced, was found in 2008 in the cave, in a pit sealed with sheep dung that preserved it. Radiocarbon dating gave it to about 3500 BC, older than the standing stones of Stonehenge and some centuries older than the shoes of Ötzi the Iceman, making it the oldest known leather shoe.
entries.note: R. Pinhasi et al., 'First direct evidence of Chalcolithic footwear from the Near Eastern Highlands', PLoS ONE 5 (2010).

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The first hominins outside Africa, obsidian circulation, a hunter-gatherer ancestry that spread north, and Mesopotamian contact

entries.label: Dmanisi and the dispersal from Africa
entries.hint: The Dmanisi fossils are the best evidence that Homo reached the temperate zone of Eurasia very early, before the Acheulean hand-axe and with a brain not much larger than that of its ancestors. Their discoverers read the Caucasus as a staging post on the route from Africa through the Levant to Asia and Europe.
entries.note: Gabunia et al., Science 288 (2000); Lordkipanidze et al. 2013; Ferring et al., PNAS 108 (2011).

entries.label: The Caucasus ancestry in Eurasia
entries.hint: The genome of the Caucasus hunter-gatherers is a major component in later populations of the Pontic–Caspian steppe, in the Yamnaya herders of about 3000 BC, and in the farmers of Iran and Armenia. The Caucasus thus appears as a corridor and a source of a contributor to the ancestry of present-day Europeans and West Asians.
entries.note: Jones et al. 2015; W. Haak et al., Nature 522 (2015); Lazaridis et al. 2016.

entries.label: Contact with Mesopotamia and the north
entries.loc: Leyla Tepe and the Maykop region
entries.hint: The painted pottery of Leyla Tepe has parallels at Ubaid sites in northern Mesopotamia, and in the later fourth millennium the Caucasus is in contact with the Late Uruk world to the south and the Maykop culture of the Kuban to the north. Metal ores, obsidian and pottery styles were what travelled.
entries.note: Lyonnet et al. 2012; Rothman (ed.), Uruk Mesopotamia and Its Neighbors (2001).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The glacial refuge, the Holocene warming and the wetter plains

entries.label: The Caucasus as an Ice Age refuge
entries.hint: In the Last Glacial Maximum the high Caucasus carried glaciers and the northern steppes were cold desert, while the valleys of the south and the Colchian lowlands remained forested and wet. Plants, animals and humans were gathered in the refuge, which explains the long isolation of the Caucasus hunter-gatherer population seen in the genomes.
entries.note: Jones et al. 2015; palaeoclimate reviews of the Caucasus.

entries.label: The Holocene warming and the wetter plains
entries.hint: After the end of the Younger Dryas cold around 9600 BC the climate warmed and became more moist, and the river plains, which had been steppe, filled with marsh and woodland on the Kura and Araxes. Wild cereals and grapes spread, and permanent villages on alluvial fans became possible.
entries.note: L. Wick et al., The Holocene 13 (2003), on the Lake Van record; regional palaeoclimate reviews.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: A hominin who lived years without teeth, and children buried beneath the floors

entries.label: The hominin without teeth
entries.hint: One Dmanisi skull, the D3444, belongs to an old individual who had lost nearly all of his teeth some years before death, and the bone of the jaw had healed. He survived on soft food and probably the help of others, an early case of care of the disabled, as argued by Lordkipanidze and colleagues.
entries.note: D. Lordkipanidze et al., 'The earliest toothless hominin skull', Nature 434 (2005).

entries.label: Children of the village
entries.hint: Children and infants make up a large share of the burials of the Neolithic villages, as in other farming settlements of the Near East, and infant mortality was clearly high. Their graves, with small ornaments, beads and pots, are among the few traces of ordinary lives.
entries.note: Badalyan et al.; Chataigner et al. 2014.
